newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ govt spend-up will pressure inflation - Treasury.
newsitem.headline: NZ govt spend-up will pressure inflation - Treasury.

text.p: The NZ$5 billion in extra government spending in the coalition agreement is likely to add to inflationary pressure and increase the risks of a change in international sentiment toward New Zealand, according to Treasury advice to the government.

The New Zealand Press Association reported on Wednesday that the March 11 secret budget document, released to NZPA under the Official Information Act, also predicted tighter monetary conditions from mid-year, a higher exchange rate and higher current account deficit.
Treasury said that the projections for potential growth of 3-3.5 percent, the economy's sustainable rate of growth, remained unchanged, NZPA reported.

However, it said that given its assessment that there was minimal spare capacity in the economy, "higher government spending is likely to add to inflation pressures rather than increase economic growth".
The higher inflation pressures meant that monetary conditions needed to be tighter than they otherwise need to be.
"We expect monetary conditions to tighten from around the middle of the year."
It was likely the exchange rate would rise and bear at least some of the burden of keeping inflation under control in the face of government spending.
"This may dampen net exports but reduce the need for higher interest rates."
As a result, the current account deficit was likely to be higher than forecast in the December Economic and Fiscal Update (DEFU).
"This increases the risk of a change in sentiment towards New Zealand and the risk of both a currency re-alignment and a rise in the cost of capital."

The DEFU forecast a current account deficit of 4.5 percent of GDP in 1996/97. The deficit, which measures New Zealand's international trade and transactions, reached 4.2 percent of GDP in December quarter data released last week.

The document was prepared for Treasurer Winston Peters as part of an initial assessment of the impact of the coalition agreement and recent economic data on the economic projections of DEFU, NZPA said.

It takes into account the deferral of the tax cuts and the extra government expenditure over three years, does not include the potential impacts of a compulsory superannuation scheme or proposed tax cuts in 1999.
The Reserve Bank has maintained unchanged monetary conditions for most of this year but has said government spending plans contribute importantly to inflation in late 1998 and 1999.
Peters has argued that the extra spending did not amount to significant fiscal easing and that it was considered to be prudent, given current conditions.

In the March 4 budget policy statement he and Finance Minister Bill Birch emphasised the government's commitment to price stability and acknowledged that only additional spending or tax cuts beyond what was promised in the coalition agreement would likely lead to higher interest rates and exchange rates.
Treasury said in its briefing paper that higher government spending at a time when there were few spare resources, would displace private sector consumption and investment spending.
"This has partly been achieved through delaying the tax cuts, but works more generally through tighter monetary conditions which are required to keep inflation under control."
Any additional government spending beyond that set out in the coalition agreement would put pressure on monetary conditions to tighten further, Treasury warned.

Treasury also said the effect on economic growth of widening the inflation target from the previous 0-2 percent target to 0-3 percent was assumed to be "negligible" because of the small increase in the mid-point target.
However, if inflationary expectation increased by more than 0.5 percent as a result, then the Reserve Bank would have to keep monetary conditions tighter.
